'''''Echeveria agavoides''''', or 'lipstick' echeveria, is a [[species]] of [[Succulent plant|succulent]] [[flowering plant]] of the stonecrop ([[sedum]]) [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Crassulaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to the rocky canyons and arid hillsides of [[Mexican Plateau|Central Mexico]]. It is primarily known from the states of [[Aguascalientes]], [[Durango]], [[Guanajuato]], [[Hidalgo (state)|Hidalgo]], [[Jalisco]], [[Querétaro]], [[San Luis Potosí]] and [[Zacatecas]], though it has been sighted as far north as [[Coahuila]] and as far south as [[Oaxaca]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Observations • iNaturalist |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6793&subview=map&taxon_id=282740 |access-date=19 May 2024 |website=[[iNaturalist]].org}}</ref>

==Description==
''Echeveria agavoides'' is a small, stemless [[succulent plant|succulent]] plant, {{convert|8|-|12|cm}} tall, with a rosette of leaves {{convert|7|-|15|cm}} in diameter. It is often solitary, but old plants in good condition grow offsets. The leaves are green, triangular, thicker (6 mm) and more acute than the other echeverias - hence the explanation of their name ''agavoides'', "looking like an agave".<ref>{{cite book|author=Harrison, Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref> Some varieties with bright light have reddish (or bronze) tips and some forms have slightly red to very red margins. The inflorescences in summer appear on slender, single-sided [[cyme (botany)|cymes]] up to {{convert|50|cm}} long. The flowers are pink, orange or red, the petals tipped with dark yellow.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref>

==Etymology==
''Echeveria'' is named for [[Atanasio Echeverría y Godoy]], a botanical illustrator who contributed to ''Flora Mexicana''.<ref name="gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp. 39, 149</ref>

''Agavoides'' means 'resembling ''[[Agave]]''.'<ref name="gledhill" />

==Taxonomy==
Varieties:<ref name=POWO_273738-1/>
*''Echeveria agavoides'' var. ''agavoides''
*''Echeveria agavoides'' var. ''corderoyi'' <small>(Baker) Poelln.</small>
*''Echeveria agavoides'' var. ''multifida'' <small>E.Walther</small>
*''Echeveria agavoides'' var. ''prolifera'' <small>E.Walther</small>

Cultivars:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.truesucculents.com/search?type=product%2Carticle%2Cpage&q=NOT+tag%3A__gift+AND+Agavoides* |title=True Succulents; Agavoides hybrids and cultivars|publisher=TrueSucculents.com official site |accessdate=5 December 2022}}</ref>
*'Aquamarine', with icy, emerald-green leaves.
*'Ebony', lighter-coloured leaves (almost beige or peach) with dark brown edges, almost burgundy.
*'Lipstick', neon green leaves with irregular red leaf edges.
*'Luming', with reddish, maroon-magenta leaves, maturing to dark purple; also has rather pointed leaves.
*'Oculus', with an entirely burgundy-reddish colour.
*'Rose Garnet', faint neon-green leaves of rather large and sturdy shape, tipped with magenta pink and maturing to red.
*'Rubra', with dark reddish leaves growing in a notably tight, almost "closed" rosette.
*'Salu' grows in a considerably tighter, closed rosette, with pale green leaves lightly tipped in red. Small "point" to the ends of the leaves, which mature to red.

==Cultivation==
As with most echeverias, ''E. agavoides'' may be harmed by moisture and prefers mineral soils, growing best in light and even direct sunshine, which aids flowering. In order to flower, plants need rest in the winter, without water and in a cold place - but not less than {{convert|5|C}}. In [[temperateness|temperate]] regions they must be kept indoors during winter, but may be placed outside during the summer months.<ref name=RHSAZ/>

This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Echeveria agavoides''|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=2850|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121224034330/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=2850|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 24, 2012|accessdate=18 June 2013}}</ref>

Many hybrids have been created to obtain more brightly colored flowers or leaves.

The easiest methods of [[plant propagation|propagation]] are leaf cuttings and division of older plants. It propagates easily from cutting the stem although propagation from leaves can be more difficult. In order to propagate, one must take a sharp sterilized knife or scissors to cut away at the stem or leaves. Time must pass to allow for callousing before replanting.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.succulentsandsunshine.com/types-of-succulents/echeveria-agavoides-lipstick-echeveria/|title=This Echeveria shows off when it's been happily "stressed."|date=2019-02-09|website=Succulents and Sunshine|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-23}}</ref>
